reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
clinicalPearls: An abnormal communication between the carotid arterial system and the cavernous sinus, which arterialises the venous sinus and its tributaries
Classified as direct (high-flow, often traumatic or from a ruptured intracavernous carotid aneurysm) or indirect (dural, low-flow, arising spontaneously, often in older women or with hypertension)
The classic triad is pulsatile proptosis, chemosis, and an ocular or orbital bruit; a whooshing noise in the head is often reported

Arterialisation of orbital veins produces dilated conjunctival (corkscrew) vessels, raised intraocular pressure, and ophthalmoplegia from involvement of the cranial nerves in the sinus, and can threaten vision
Direct high-flow fistulae usually present dramatically after head trauma, whereas indirect dural fistulae are more insidious with a red eye that can mimic conjunctivitis or thyroid eye disease
Diagnosis uses orbital imaging (CT or MRI showing a dilated superior ophthalmic vein and an enlarged cavernous sinus) with catheter angiography as the definitive study
Management is usually endovascular closure (transarterial or transvenous embolisation); some low-flow dural fistulae close spontaneously or after manual carotid compression
reference.pathophysiology: A carotid-cavernous fistula is an abnormal shunt between the carotid artery and the cavernous sinus. In direct fistulae a tear in the intracavernous internal carotid artery, from trauma or a ruptured aneurysm, allows high-pressure arterial blood directly into the sinus; in indirect (dural) fistulae, meningeal branches of the internal or external carotid feed the sinus at low flow. Arterial pressure within the cavernous sinus reverses venous drainage and engorges and arterialises the orbital veins. This raises orbital, episcleral, and intraocular pressure, produces proptosis, chemosis, and a bruit, and compromises the cranial nerves traversing the sinus to cause ophthalmoplegia; venous congestion and ocular ischaemia can threaten sight.
additionalDifferentials: Conjunctivitis or scleritis (for the red eye of an indirect fistula)
Orbital pseudotumour or inflammatory orbital disease
additionalInvestigations: CT and MRI of the orbits and brain (dilated superior ophthalmic vein, bulging cavernous sinus, proptosis)
CT or MR angiography to demonstrate the fistula
Catheter (digital subtraction) cerebral angiography as the definitive diagnostic and treatment-planning study
Measurement of intraocular pressure and ophthalmic assessment of vision and ocular motility
Orbital colour Doppler ultrasound showing arterialised flow in the superior ophthalmic vein
Assessment for cortical venous drainage or reflux, which indicates higher risk
redFlags: Deteriorating visual acuity or signs of ocular ischaemia (sight-threatening)
Cortical venous drainage or reflux indicating a risk of intracranial haemorrhage
Rapidly worsening proptosis or new cranial nerve palsies
reference.prognosis: Indirect low-flow dural fistulae may resolve spontaneously or after conservative measures, whereas direct high-flow fistulae usually require endovascular treatment; with timely closure the ocular signs generally regress, but delayed treatment risks permanent visual loss.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the red eye of an indirect fistula as conjunctivitis or thyroid eye disease
Missing the diagnosis when no bruit is audible in a low-flow fistula
Overlooking cortical venous reflux that raises the risk of haemorrhage
Delaying imaging or angiography in a patient with progressive visual loss
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
management: Endovascular closure by transarterial or transvenous embolisation with detachable coils, balloons or liquid embolic agents as definitive treatment for direct high-flow fistulae
Conservative measures including intermittent manual carotid compression for low-flow indirect dural fistulae, many of which thrombose spontaneously
Control of raised intraocular pressure with topical ocular hypotensive agents and regular ophthalmic monitoring of vision and ocular motility
Urgent intervention where there is deteriorating vision or cortical venous drainage or reflux, indicating a high risk of haemorrhage
Treatment of the underlying cause, such as securing a ruptured intracavernous carotid aneurysm
Post-treatment surveillance imaging to confirm closure and detect recurrence
Multidisciplinary care involving interventional neuroradiology, ophthalmology and neurosurgery
